title: Calibration: aligning stated confidence with actual accuracy

videos.script: Ask a model how sure it is, and it gives you a number. Point nine seven, say. It looks like a probability. It is text the model wrote, like everything else in the answer. {{number}} This lesson asks whether that number means anything. On one message the stand-in says point nine seven, and it is wrong. {{h04}} One mistake proves nothing about a confidence. So you group seventy answers by what they claimed, and count how often each group was right. {{bins}} That gives you the picture this topic is known for. Stated confidence along one side, accuracy up the other, and a diagonal where the two agree. Every point lands below it. {{diagram}} Then you put a number on the gap, two ways, and you use the confidence for something. A threshold chosen on the easy set promises perfect answers. On the hard set it delivers two in three. {{threshold}} By the end you know how to measure a stated confidence, and why you never simply trust one. {{close}}
